title: College Softball’s Best Lineups (2021–2022)
text:
One superstar can change an inning, but winning a conference or reaching Oklahoma City takes an entire batting order. Across 479 full NCAA Division I team-seasons in 2021 and 2022 (programs with at least 7 qualifying hitters in the dataset), the typical college lineup posted an .802 weighted OPS—combining a .363 On-Base Percentage (OBP) with a .439 Slugging Percentage (SLG).
Yet colleges built dangerous lineups using very different blueprints:

title: Inside NCAA Division I Softball Hitting (2021–2022)
text:
Welcome! In college softball, putting the bat on the ball is the first test of every offense—yet across 4,406 individual player-seasons and 302 NCAA Division I programs in 2021 and 2022, hitters succeeded in very different ways. Start with the two interactive Batting Average vs. Strikeouts charts below, inspect the hitters who beat the red trendline, and explore the rest of the site to see how lineups, power, transfers, and speed fit together.

Jump to Chart Outlier Explorer ↓ Compare Players Head-to-Head Browse Top Lineups

title: Inside NCAA Division I Softball Hitting (2021–2022)
text:
2021 Batting Average vs. Strikeouts
How does striking out (K) relate to batting average (BA—the share of official at-bats that result in a hit)? Hover over any dot on the 2021 and 2022 charts below to see a player’s name, college, batting average, and strikeout total, or drag a box to zoom in on crowded clusters.






In the 2021 season (2,131 players), the typical player hit .280 (getting a hit in 28% of their at-bats) and struck out about 19 times. Each additional 10 strikeouts along the downward-sloping red line corresponded to roughly a 14-point drop (-.014) in batting average, though plenty of everyday hitters stayed well above the red line even with 20 to 40 strikeouts.

title: Inside NCAA Division I Softball Hitting (2021–2022)
text:
2022 Batting Average vs. Strikeouts






In the 2022 season (2,275 players), the average batting average stayed nearly identical at .278, while strikeouts climbed to 23 per player as teams returned to full post-pandemic schedules. Just like in 2021, every +10 strikeouts lowered expected batting average by about 15 points (-.015), dropping off steepest past 40 strikeouts.

title: About
text:
About the Data
The data used throughout this website comes from the SCORE Sports Data Repository: NCAA Division I Softball Batting (2021–2022), part of the SCORE Network collection of sports datasets curated from official NCAA Division I Softball Statistics. Together, the 2021 (batting2021.csv, 2,131 players) and 2022 (batting2022.csv, 2,275 players) files cover 4,406 qualifying player-seasons across 302 Division I programs, recording plate appearances, hits, extra-base hits, home runs, walks, strikeouts, stolen bases, and rate statistics (BA, OBP, SLG, and OPS).

text:

title: Sluggers & Strikeouts
text:
On the Home page, striking out looks like plain bad news: players with more strikeouts generally end up with lower batting averages (meaning they get hits less often). However, batting average counts a soft single and a game-winning home run as the exact same thing. When we look at all 4,406 college softball player seasons from 2021 and 2022 and count home runs instead, we see the opposite pattern: players who hit the most home runs usually strike out more than average, because swinging hard for the fences comes with more swings and misses.









In the chart above, each dot is a player’s season, and darker purple dots mark stronger overall hitters (measured by OPS, a single rating that combines how often a batter reaches base and how far they hit the ball). For most big sluggers, power comes with a clear trade-off. To the right of the dashed average line (21 strikeouts), stars like Wichita State’s Addison Barnard (33 home runs, 37 strikeouts) and Miami (OH)’s Karli Spaid (28 home runs, 39 strikeouts) struck out nearly twice as often as a typical player, yet more than made up for those outs by driving the ball over the fence.
Then there is Oklahoma’s Jocelyn Alo, sitting at the very top left of the chart, who ignored that trade-off completely. In both 2021 and 2022, Alo led the entire country with 34 home runs while striking out just 16 and 19 times—fewer strikeouts than an average college player who hit fewer than four home runs all season. By 2022, opposing pitchers were so afraid to throw strikes to her that she walked 54 times and still got a hit in more than half of her official at-bats, breaking the all-time college career home run record (122 homers). Alongside teammate Tiare Jennings—who also crushed 29 home runs with only 13 strikeouts in 2022—Alo helped make Oklahoma nearly impossible to pitch to, powering the Sooners to back-to-back national championships.





Putting Oklahoma’s Run in Perspective (2021–2022)
Over these two seasons, a typical Division I softball hitter averaged about 4 home runs and 21 strikeouts per year. Oklahoma teammates Jocelyn Alo and Tiare Jennings combined for 124 home runs while striking out only 65 times total across both years—giving the Sooners historic power without giving away easy outs on their way to two straight Women’s College World Series titles.

title: Speed & Power on 60-Foot Bases
text:
In NCAA Division I softball, where bases sit just 60 feet apart, base stealers succeed 83.5% of the time (21,328 steals in 25,535 tries across 2021 and 2022). Yet hitting for power and stealing bases usually belong to completely different types of players.
To make that L-shaped split easy to see without thousands of low-volume bench rows cluttering the corner, the two charts below focus on college softball’s standout power and speed threats—every player who either hit 10+ home runs or stole 15+ bases:

title: Speed & Power on 60-Foot Bases
text:
2021 Season: Speed vs. Power






In 2021 (331 standout hitters), notice how cleanly the blue and green dots separate along the two axes: Oklahoma’s Jocelyn Alo sits high on the left (34 HRs, 0 SBs), while Central Arkansas’s Jenna Wildeman stretches all the way to the right along zero (0 HRs, 56 SBs). Only 13 players in the country reached the red dual-threat zone, led by Miami (OH)’s Karli Spaid (17 HRs, 19 SBs) and Eastern Illinois’s Megan Burton (19 HRs, 17 SBs).

title: Speed & Power on 60-Foot Bases
text:
2022 Season: Speed vs. Power






In 2022 (433 standout hitters), the dual-threat group grew to 16 players—highlighted by Wichita State’s Addison Barnard, who sits way up in the top middle with 33 home runs and 25 stolen bases, alongside Northwestern’s Rachel Lewis (23 HRs, 25 SBs) and Tennessee’s Kiki Milloy (15 HRs, 31 SBs). Meanwhile, USF speedster Alexis Johns pushed pure base stealing even further on the bottom right with 59 steals in 61 tries and zero home runs.
